SiteSense

AI-powered Retail Expansion Intelligence Platform · Pune
Triwizathon · Problem Statement 1
Suyash Patil · Harshad Khatale · Tanuja Saravale · Madanaj Sagar
Walchand College of Engineering

1. The problem statement

Problem Statement 1 - Retail Expansion Intelligence Platform. Choosing the right place for a new store is hard. A location may have many people but also strong competition, high rent or poor access. Doing this by manual research or gut feeling leads to poor investments and missed chances.

In simple words

A retail chain wants to open its next shop. There are thousands of possible places in a city. Which place will earn the most, which are risky, and why? We must build software that answers this with data and AI, and explains its answer.

Figure 1. A location is never good or bad on one factor. The platform must weigh all of these together.

What the challenge asks, and where we answer it

2. Our solution

SiteSense tells a retail owner where to open the next store. It splits Pune into small hexagons, measures what surrounds each one, learns what successful locations look like, simulates how customers would choose between stores, and explains every recommendation in plain language. The owner picks a business type and limits; the app does the rest.

Figure 2. The six steps from raw data to an explained recommendation.

Figure 3. The working app: guided steps (left), hexagon map with ranked pins, and plain-language results.

What the owner does

  1. Choose the business (or just type: “best 3 pharmacy sites near Baner under 60 lakh”).
  2. Set limits: start-up money, highest rent, area, store size.
  3. Pick what matters: balanced, max profit, play it safe, or best market fit.
  4. Add existing stores by clicking the map, so new sites do not steal their sales.
  5. Read the answer: top sites with a weak / likely / strong profit range, reasons, risks and confidence.
  6. Test it: what if rent rises 30%, or a rival opens next door? Or plan 2-6 stores together.

Why it is different

  • Honest ranges, never a single made-up number.
  • Explainable: each site lists its top reasons and risks.
  • Category-aware: a pharmacy and a fashion store need different things (the “Retail DNA”).
  • Transparent data: every value says if it is real or estimated.

Figure 4. How the engine narrows the whole city to a short list (shown live in the app).

2.1 How the AI works

There is no sales data for any shop in the area, so we avoid pretending. We learn from where established chains already trade (a weak but real signal), test the models on whole neighbourhoods they never saw, and simulate sales with stated assumptions.

PartWhat it doesTechnique
Opportunity index (BOI)Scores every zone 0-100 on 10 factors; the weights differ per business (the “Retail DNA”).Simple weighted formula - fully explainable
Viability modelLearns what proven locations look like. “Proven” = an established chain outlet already trades in the zone.XGBoost, positive-unlabeled learning
Location rankerOrders zones from best to worst for each business; higher rent never raises a score.LightGBM LambdaRank
Rent modelSpreads 35 known locality rents to every zone, with a likely range.CatBoost + validation on unseen localities
Profit simulationShoppers split their spending between stores by distance and attractiveness; repeated 300 times with uncertain inputs.Huff gravity model + Monte Carlo
CannibalisationEstimates how much of a new store’s sales would come from your own nearby stores.Same gravity model
ExplanationsTurns model contributions into plain reasons, risk flags and a confidence level.SHAP + rules
Zone typesGroups areas into 6 types (office hub, student belt, high street…).K-means on PCA
Expansion plannerChooses the best set of stores together, within budget and spacing.OR-Tools CP-SAT
Ask in EnglishTurns a sentence into a safe, whitelisted search.Rule-based parser (no chatbot)

The “Retail DNA”: what matters for each business

Figure 5. Weights (0-100, each column adds up to 100). Darker = matters more. Stored in a config file, shown in the app.

How a score and a profit are made

Opportunity score = Σ weight × factor score ÷ 100, for the 10 factors.
Bands: Prime 80+Strong 65-79Viable 50-64Marginal 35-49Avoid <35
Profit = sales × margin − rent − fixed costs.
Sales = what each nearby neighbourhood spends × the share this store wins against rivals, summed over the catchment. Repeated 300 times with varied spend, margin, rent, distance sensitivity and number of unmapped stores. We report the 10th, 50th and 90th percentile and the chance of profit.
Safeguards: the defining chain outlet is hidden from the model’s inputs (no cheating); every zone is scored by a model that never saw its neighbourhood; rent can only lower a score; a plain-index fallback is used when labels are too few.

5. Feasibility

Technical feasibility: it already runs

  • Full pipeline works end to end on real Pune data and builds in about 5 minutes.
  • A search finishes in seconds on a laptop; unit tests cover the gravity maths (more rivals never raise sales, own stores cause overlap).
  • Only free tools and open data are used - no paid API is needed.

Does the learning work? (tested on unseen neighbourhoods)

“Of the zones that really host an established chain, how many land in the model’s top 10%?”

Figure 8. Share of proven zones found in the top 10% (higher is better). Random guessing scores 10%. Sports has too few labels to test.

The learned model beats a population-only rule and a plain index in every business it was tested on (e.g. pharmacy 52% vs 8% for population only). These checks show the model finds chain-like locations; they are not proof of profit.

5.1 Viability: would it be useful and sustainable?

Who needs it and why

  • Retail chains and franchise owners who open stores every year and today rely on brokers and gut feeling.
  • Small entrepreneurs choosing a first shop, who cannot afford consultants.
  • Real-estate and mall teams who want to judge which tenant fits a location.

It saves research time, makes trade-offs visible (rent vs footfall vs rivals) and shows why, so decisions can be defended to investors.

How it can sustain itself

  • Software subscription per chain or per city.
  • Paid reports for a single location decision.
  • Premium data upload: a client’s real sales make the model far better.

Why it can scale

  • A new city = one YAML file and a rebuild; a new business = one block of weights, tags and economics.
  • Open data, no per-user data cost; all heavy work is pre-computed.

Honest limitations

  • No real sales data. Profit comes from a simulation with our assumptions (spend per person, margins, store density). It is decision support, not a guarantee.
  • “Proven” means a chain is there, not that it is profitable.
  • OpenStreetMap is incomplete. Only 25 sports shops are mapped in Pune, so sports uses the plain index and shows lower confidence.
  • Rent model is basic. On unseen localities it is off by about 15%, similar to a simple price rule (14%).
  • Growth data was unavailable at build time, so the growth factor is neutral and flagged.
  • Population is a modelled 1 km raster; prices come from a 35-locality table; the study area is a rectangle (not the exact city border); no zoning, lease or online-demand data.

Next steps

  • Clip the grid to the real city boundary; retry growth data.
  • Calibrate with real sales from one pilot chain.
  • Add live rent listings and footfall data; more cities.
  • Fast surrogate models, a learned growth forecaster, user accounts and PDF reports.
